newsitem.title: USA: Stock market expected to take a breather.
newsitem.headline: Stock market expected to take a breather.

text.p: The stock market is expected to take a breather and consolidate their gains at least for the first few days of this holiday shortened week after Dow Jones industrial average topped the 7,000 millennium mark for the first time last Thursday.
Analysts say they would welcome any respite after last week's gains to reduce the market's overbought condition and bring valuations down a bit.
Some said that with the recent losses in high technology stocks, particularly among computer networkers, momentum traders are finding themselves with fewer stocks to use as investment vehicles.
Trading will begin Tuesday after the conclusion of the three-day Presidents' Day weekend. On Friday, the Dow closed down 33.48 points at 6,988.96 after posting a gain for the week of 133 points.

Grace Messner, vice president of equity management at Wilmington Trust, said that with most of the major economic data for January are out, and there are no particular near-term catalysts to drive the market higher.

"It's hard to point to any event that will push us lower, but I think because we are so vulnerable at this level that there is plenty of room for a nasty surprise," she said. "Whether this will happen this week or next month, I have no idea. But the market looks like it is exhausting itself."
Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons, said that a pullback to as low as 6,850 on the Dow would do the market little harm and quite a bit of good at this point.

"A pause is not only normal but healthy because it removes price excesses and makes it easier to buy stocks,"he said. "You don't want to be buying stocks while they are hitting new highs. Even if they move just a point down you feel better about it."
Investors will continue to focus on the groups, which have been in the forefront of the stock market rally -- financial, drug and high technology stocks.
But not all technology stocks. The recent sharp losses in the networking sector have changed the environment for investment in technology issues, analysts said.

"We are seeing a separation between good techs and bad techs," O'Bryan said. Among "strong stocks" in the group, he named Intel Corp., Microsoft Corp., Dell Computer Corp. and International Business Machines Corp., while listing others that are "stumbling," such as 3Com Corp. and Cascade Communications Corp.
"This is still a strong area, but you have to forget about the stocks that have really been crushed," O'Bryan said. "Don't touch them. You can get hurt catching a falling knife."
The recent trouncing of several high-profile networkers has also scared momentum traders out of the area, said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"The carnage in the information technology industry has limited the number of vehicles that momentum players can utilize," he said. "This has forced even more money into a smaller universe of blue chips, like the drugs and consumer staple demand stocks. The area has become overcrowded, stretched and quite vulnerable."
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross, said that the market's performance depended heavily on the flow of cash into mutual funds.

"That has been the driving force of the market over the past few months even more than the fundamentals," he said. "We are in an environment in which bad news is good news for the market and good news is good news for the market, too. It's a money thing that is happening right now."
Data this week include the January Consumer Price Index on Tuesday and January housing starts due on Thursday.
